We evaluate SPARC on partially observable continuous control, POPGym memory benchmarks, sequence classification, and language modeling. SPARC places among the top two means across all ten reinforcement-learning tasks. Compared with RG-LRU, it improves permuted-MNIST and sequential-CIFAR-10 accuracy by $10.13$ and $10.66$ percentage points, respectively, reduces held-out language-model perplexity by $2.00\%$, and accelerates mixer forward--backward computation by up to $1.69\times$ at width $D=2048$. Code is available at https://github.com/Botwwt/sparc.

title: Linear Recurrent Memory Suffices to Distil a World-Model Policy for Robot Air Hockey
authors: F. Olivia Fan, Oliver Obst
abstract: Does memory-dependent control need nonlinear recurrent dynamics? We study simulated air-hockey defence under temporary loss of puck tracking. A DreamerV3 teacher outperforms a memoryless policy under tracking loss, and erasing its recurrent state at the moment tracking fails cuts its save rate sharply, so the task requires memory. We distil this teacher into compact recurrent policies with a 64-dimensional state, combining a diagonal linear recurrence with an optional rank-$k$ nonlinear innovation while the observation encoder and action head stay nonlinear. Across five matched seeds, the purely linear recurrent model ($k=0$) matches both the GRU baseline and the teacher throughout the tested range of tracking loss. Increasing nonlinear innovation rank provides no measured benefit. This result comes from a fresh test split that was opened only after all models and analyses were frozen. Under 5\,mm observation noise, without retraining, the linear student keeps a higher save rate than the GRU baseline, while using fewer recurrent parameters and less computation. These results suggest that, for this memory-dependent control task, nonlinear representation learning around a simple linear memory can be sufficient, and that nonlinear recurrent dynamics are not necessarily required.

title: Physics-Informed GMDH for Adaptive Field Reconstruction
authors: Mykhailo Minin
abstract: Physics-informed computational methods usually optimize parameters within a functional representation whose structure is fixed in advance. This work proposes a Physics-Informed Method of Group Data Handling (PI-GMDH), in which representations of coupled physical fields are progressively constructed during solution. Candidate functional directions are evaluated through the first variation of the complete physical and observational objective, introduced in packages, and followed by block-coordinate damped Gauss-Newton coefficient optimization. The framework is demonstrated with tensor-product Chebyshev functions on the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations using a two-dimensional time-dependent Taylor-Green benchmark. Under the tested configuration, adaptive PI-GMDH reached validation and held-out test losses of 5.299e-19 and 5.296e-19 with 204, 201, and 175 active functions for u, v, and p. Complete degree-by-degree and all-terms PI-GMDH variants, together with selected PINN and KAN reference configurations, are used to examine the effect of structural construction policy. The Taylor-Green experiments demonstrate that package-wise structural-growth policies can substantially affect the attained reconstruction accuracy, representation size, and computational cost under the tested configuration. These results support PI-GMDH as a self-organizing basis-construction framework for physics-informed regression and field reconstruction; they do not separately establish the advantage of its candidate-scoring mechanism or general superiority over other physics-informed approaches.

title: MADGRAV: a multilevel anomaly-detection pipeline for gravitational-wave searches applied to LIGO data
authors: Gianluca Inguglia, Huw Haigh, Ulyana Dupletsa, Alessandro Longo
abstract: We present the results of \textbf{MADGRAV}, a deep-learning-based search for high-mass compact binary coalescences, applied to the data collected by the LIGO interferometers during the third observing run and during the first and second part of the fourth observing run. The \textbf{MADGRAV} pipeline consists of a series of sequential convolutional neural networks that perform anomaly detection, glitch classification, coherence testing, and signal ranking. Data from the Hanford and Livingston LIGO detectors are studied (both individually and in coherence) by way of 1 second Q-transform windows. Of the candidates that survive every stage of the pipeline, 48 reach the significance threshold, and we report 47 gravitational wave detections characterised by a false alarm rate below $1\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$ with a probability of astrophysical origin $p_{\rm astro}>0.9$. Of the 47 detections, 44 are shared with the minimally modelled coherent WaveBurst search. The observed total source-frame masses, extracted from official gravitational wave transient catalogues, are in the $14-236 M_{\odot}$ range with a median of $69 M_{\odot}$, and a median SNR of 16. We note that the recovered fraction of confident detections rises with mass: for LIGO detectors network SNR $>10$ the pipeline recovers $8.1\%$ of confident catalog events below $30 M_{\odot}$, $39.8\%$ between $30$ and $100 M_{\odot}$, and $53.3\%$ above $100 M_{\odot}$, corresponding to $33.3\%$, $45.5\%$ and $53.3\%$ of the events detected by coherent WaveBurst in the same bins. These results suggest that anomaly detection pipelines can serve as an independent detection channel complementary to matched filtering in the high-mass high-SNR regime.

title: Build2SPARQL: A Large-Scale Text-to-SPARQL Benchmark Dataset for Building Knowledge Graph Querying
authors: Wooyoung Jung
abstract: Building automation systems are increasingly represented as semantic knowledge graphs (KGs) using ontologies such as Brick and ASHRAE 223P, creating a machine-readable substrate for artificial-intelligence applications. One promising application is translating natural-language questions into SPARQL (text-to-SPARQL), which would let building operators query these graphs through language agents, but progress is limited by the scarcity of large natural-language/SPARQL benchmarks. This paper presents Build2SPARQL, a large-scale benchmark for building KGs generated by a KG-grounded pipeline: SPARQL queries are produced and validated entirely by graph-traversal code, while large language models generate only the natural-language questions, keeping query correctness independent of model behavior. The pipeline mines six query-pattern families -- linear chains, branching, UNION, aggregation, OPTIONAL, and attribute-filtered -- and phrases each query across five vocabulary registers. Applied to 201 building KGs (180 Brick, 21 ASHRAE 223P), it yields 6,136 executable SPARQL queries and 30,680 questions. A two-rater human validation of 300 questions found 98.8% semantic fidelity, 98.8% naturalness, and 84.0% operational plausibility. A retrieval-augmented evaluation across three open-weight language models raised exact-match accuracy from 0.2-20% (zero-shot) to 56-65% (three-shot retrieved).

title: One-Step Generative Modeling via Training Dynamics Action
authors: Zhangyong Liang, Ying Huang, Haibin Ling
abstract: Recent one-step generators learn to move outputs toward data by fitting sample movements. However, the optimizer updates shared parameters rather than sample positions, so the movements can differ from those prescribed. To address this issue, we propose Training Dynamics Action (TDAC), which uses the cost of fitting movements jointly to choose transport plans. For a linearized generator, local generator action is the minimum sum of parameter-update cost and a feature-fitting penalty over shared parameter increments. We derive a closed-form action and minimize a regularized version while retaining a prescribed fraction of the reference plan's predicted distributional improvement. We estimate the covariance of feature responses using random parameter directions and evaluate action with a low-rank approximation. The plan defines fixed regression targets. An execution-gap bound relates local generator action to first-order progress of the actual update. Planning occurs during training; inference requires one generator evaluation. On ImageNet 256 x 256, TDAC achieves Frechet Inception Distance (FID) below 1.1 without distillation. Furthermore, TDAC reduces optimizer-time action while maintaining distributional accuracy and full mode coverage. At comparable FID, TDAC requires approximately 100 times fewer generator evaluations than multi-step diffusion models. The code for our work will be released soon.

title: Joint neural inference of dynamics and noise covariance for SDEs driven by weighted sub-fractional Brownian motion
authors: J. H. Ramirez-Gonzalez, Raul Astudillo
abstract: We develop a computational procedure for jointly estimating drift, diffusion, temporal covariance weight, and covariance exponent from discrete observations of stochastic differential equations driven by weighted sub-fractional Brownian motion. A change of variables in the Euler recursion yields a trajectory likelihood that retains dependence between Gaussian driving increments and includes the Jacobian associated with state-dependent diffusion. The estimator combines neural-network and radial-basis representations with analytic covariance assembly for piecewise-constant temporal weights. Normalizing the temporal weight separates its global scale from that of diffusion. For each candidate exponent, the optimal global diffusion rescaling is obtained in closed form, leaving a one-dimensional profile search. We compare the procedure with two neural likelihood adaptations on identical simulated trajectories across twenty coefficient settings. Under the specified training schedules, it attains the smallest exponent, diffusion, and temporal-weight errors in 19, 16, and 14 settings, respectively. Drift performance is mixed, with the smallest error in ten settings. These results assess the complete estimation procedures under the prescribed observation design and training schedules.

title: World-Model Gradient Refinement in CEM: An Empirical Study
authors: Shizhe Cai, Frieder Stolzenburg, Oliver Obst
abstract: The cross-entropy method (CEM) uses world-model predictions both to select action sequences and to determine where to sample next. We isolate the effect of an early update by replacing only the first model-ranked elite set with environment-ranked elites. This fixed-state intervention lowers the selected sequence's realised tracking cost in all 12 Walker/Cheetah task-seed units. We then study short gradient updates to top-ranked candidates as a way to improve search under the model's own objective. Across 52 frozen TD-MPC2 checkpoints from 32 tasks, we compare refinement with additional CEM sampling at the same planning budget, tuning both planners' initial proposal widths. We fix the groups before this comparison using an exploratory model-only diagnostic. Refinement gains 67.8 return points on average (95\% CI [31.9, 103.6]) on ten checkpoints with large model-predicted improvements, and 0.2 ([$-2.9$, 3.4]) on the remaining 42. The diagnostic's rank test on 24 new checkpoints fails, so the association does not establish a predictive rule. Offline analyses show local benefits on some tasks and positive estimates for both proposal refitting and final selection. End-of-search polishing also helps, leaving the need for repeated refitting unresolved.

title: Why Does Train-Validation Separation Emerge? Gradient-Allocation Dynamics in Pretrained Fine-Tuning
authors: Yuchen Li, Zongqi Fan, Ken-Tye Yong, Nguyen H. Tran
abstract: During fine-tuning, training accuracy often keeps rising after validation accuracy has levelled off. We explain this growing train-validation gap with a support-transfer account: early updates use structure shared by many examples, whereas later fitting relies increasingly on narrow structure whose benefit transfers less to held-out data, so per-example gradient allocations differentiate as the gap grows. We measure this with two readouts computed from fixed training probes alone, the pooled dispersion $D_{\mathrm{den}}$ of normalized gradient magnitudes and its within-class part $D_{\mathrm{within}}^{\mathrm{wt}}$, and derive sufficient conditions under which allocation dispersion, cross-entropy separation, and the accuracy gap grow together. In a constructed feature hierarchy, raising the sample-private feature share from .3 to .7 raises the final accuracy gap from .185 to .527, and homogenizing per-example gradient magnitudes reduces the gap mainly after substantial fitting (median full-dose changes of -4.91 to -11.79 percentage points when it starts at the three later training stages). In 90 fine-tuning runs of three language backbones on six tasks, both readouts are positively associated with the accuracy gap in every run, and $D_{\mathrm{den}}$ remains positive in 89 of 90 runs after linear detrending; 20 vision runs show the same association.

title: Beyond the Parameter Monolith: Reconstructive Memories, Executable Skills, and Residual Assembly for Language Models
authors: A. Bochkov
abstract: Can a language-model system grow its external state and use executable procedures without making every component part of one shared optimization process? We present FEM-ASM, an implemented architecture that separates neural coordination, document-state construction, and deterministic execution. Independent workers optimize document memories under a frozen codec and publish immutable, versioned artifacts. Executable skills return bounded computation results. Both enter a shared neural field through type-specific adapters, explicit support mappings, and a common residual-assembly operator. The resulting computation couples a quadratic consistency substep to a recurrent learned correction. We evaluate memory construction, controlled retrieval, positional readout, execution-result rendering, and evidence attachment with unchanged core weights. The experiments show that recoverable storage, successful retrieval, and successful neural use are distinct properties. Position-specific observations improve the tested memory and execution-result interfaces, while fixed-core attachment demonstrates that newly available evidence can affect predictions through the existing interface. The contribution is an architectural and engineering account of independently produced state participating in shared neural computation, with explicit component contracts, executable protocols, and released research artifacts.

title: Agentic AI with Structured CoT for Enhancing AI's Spatial Intelligence: Visualization and Reasoning of Rotation
authors: Uttamasha Monjoree, Wei Yan
abstract: Recent studies show that artificial intelligence (AI) with language and vision capabilities still experiences limitations in spatial reasoning. In this paper, we have studied the spatial capabilities of advanced generative AI to understand the rotations of objects in 3D space, utilizing AI's image processing and language processing features. We trained and examined the spatial intelligence of a generative Agentic AI model (GPT-5.6) to understand the spatial rotation process with rotation diagrams based on the revised Purdue Spatial Visualization Test: Visualization of Rotations (Revised PSVT:R). We improvised the Revised PSVT:R by superimposing additional graphical and contextual features to evaluate how different Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning strategies influence model performance. The results indicate that structured CoT reasoning improves the spatial reasoning performance of the base GPT-5.6 model in both datasets (PSVT:R and PSVT:R with coordinate system). We used three CoT approaches - (1) Structured CoT, (2) few-shot Structured CoT, and Structured CoT with Self-optimized Prompt. The three CoT approaches evaluated in this study showed no significant performance difference. Results showed that combining structured CoT reasoning with relevant contextual information leads to considerable improvements in VLM performance on 3D rotation tasks, demonstrating the potential of agentic AI for more effective spatial reasoning. However, when contextual information is removed, structured CoT reasoning alone provides limited improvement, and the models continue to exhibit notable difficulties in understanding spatial transformations. These findings suggest that effective spatial reasoning in VLMs relies on the integration of visual, textual, and reasoning-based information in future agentic AI systems for spatial intelligence.

title: FLAT: Smoothing the Rugged Landscape for Learnable, Sample-Efficient Traffic Calibration
authors: Haopeng Deng, Thomas He, Dayuan Wang
abstract: Calibrating microscopic traffic models for urban digital twins is an expensive black-box optimization problem: evaluating each set of car-following and lane-changing parameters requires a full simulation, limiting the evaluations available per recalibration window. Matching raw trajectories yields a rugged objective that sparse surrogates struggle to learn, reducing sequential acquisition to near-random probing. We present FLAT, which couples what to optimize with where to sample next. An eight-dimensional behavioral fingerprint smooths the parameter-error landscape, making the objective learnable from a few dozen samples; annealed lower-confidence-bound (LCB) acquisition then spends each remaining run where it most reduces error. The LCB loop supports a Gaussian process (GP), random forest (RF), or multi-layer-perceptron (MLP) ensemble. Across six heterogeneous real-world scenes, FLAT-GP achieves the lowest scene-averaged behavioral error, winning 6/6 scenes against SPSA, GA, and CMA-ES and 5/6 against TPE under the matched 100-run budget. Some baselines require up to 4.4 times as many simulations to match. Ablations show objective choice shifts final behavioral error by 80.6% on average, removing sequential LCB raises the six-scene mean by 21.7%, and surrogate choice shifts it by at most 4.2%, confirming gains trace to objective geometry and sequential allocation rather than surrogate capacity.

title: How Should Teachers Be Prepared? RL on Student-Induced States for On-Policy Distillation
authors: Xiaoyu Ma, Haoyue Liu, Zhichao Wang, Jionghao Zhu, Xiaoying Tang
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves the reasoning capabilities of small language models through token-level teacher supervision on student-generated trajectories. Yet can teachers that excel at solving problems independently also guide student reasoning effectively? Prior work shows that when student prefixes follow reasoning paths that differ from the teacher's own or contain errors, teachers can be less accurate when continuing from these prefixes than when solving problems independently. To this end, we propose Prep-OPD, which uses reinforcement learning (RL) before distillation to train the teacher to adapt to the student's existing reasoning state and correct course when errors arise. Training optimizes teacher continuations from fixed student prefixes using final-answer correctness as the reward. The prepared teacher then trains the student through trajectory guidance and token-level supervision. We evaluate Prep-OPD on eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks, using Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as the teacher and Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B as students. With the 4B teacher and 1.7B student, Prep-OPD improves average accuracy over standard OPD and the strongest baseline, Relay-OPD, by 8.28 and 2.30 percentage points, respectively. Controlled experiments further show that teacher RL conditioned on student-generated prefixes yields higher student accuracy than problem-start teacher RL with and without handoff on Qwen3-1.7B. Reusing the same prepared teacher also improves Qwen3-0.6B.

title: SearchJev: A Calibrated System-1 Model for Search Agents
authors: Congfeng Cao, Lipeng Zuo, Konstantinos Papakostas, Qiwei Xu, Songwei Xu, Qianru Meng, Lun Zhou, Zhaochun Ren, Yougang Lyu, Xiaohui Yan
abstract: Search agents repeatedly make short decisions about relevance, evidence sufficiency, and search actions. Using generative language models for these decisions introduces latency and unreliable confidence. We present SearchJev, a calibrated System-1 model that separates search decisions from System-2 reasoning and generation. Given a search state and a decision schema, SearchJev scores legal options without autoregressive output generation. We propose Soft-Label Learning for Calibrated Decisions (SLCD) to learn decision probabilities from uncertain supervision and improve the reliability of decision confidence. In a dual-system search agent, SearchJev handles short decisions and delegates uncertain judgments to System 2, which retains planning, query generation, and answer composition. We also introduce SearchDecision-Bench, a benchmark unifying six types of search decisions for training and evaluation. On SearchDecision-Bench, SearchJev improves decision quality over same-size Qwen3.5 autoregressive models, achieves 5.2-5.3 times faster decisions, and reduces average expected calibration error by 41-74%. On BrowseComp-Plus, the dual-system agents achieve a 3.7-4.7 times speedup in active search time while improving answer accuracy from 45% to up to 54%.

title: Memadapter: Counterfactual Adaptation Against Memory-induced Sycophancy
authors: Ruqing Ning, Haibo Meng, Zhishang Xiang, Zerui Chen, Jinsong Su, Xin Wang, Qinggang Zhang
abstract: Long-term memory enables LLM-based agents to retain and reuse information across tasks and sessions, supporting personalization and long-horizon interactions. However, persistent memories can also induce sycophancy, causing agents to over-align with users' historical beliefs even when they are inaccurate, outdated, or inconsistent with objective evidence. Existing mitigation methods assume that memory-induced sycophancy originates from biased or incorrect memories and attempt to reduce this risk by filtering such memories at different stages of the memory pipeline. However, in the real world, objective and correct memories can still induce sycophancy, and the same memory can warrant different influence across different contexts. To this end, we propose MemAdapter, a novel framework that adaptively integrates retrieved memories to support objective and reliable reasoning. Specifically, MemAdapter consists of three components: (i) Counterfactual Induction, which leverages counterfactual reasoning to uncover the potential risk of retrieved memories; (ii) Context-Aware Reflection, which calibrates the inferential influence of each retrieved memory in light of the current task via self-reflection; and (iii) Evidence-Based Reasoning, which grounds the final response in appropriate evidence while preserving the legitimate influence of memory. Extensive experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate that MemAdapter consistently improves memory reliability across diverse scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/DEEP-JLU/MemAdapter.

title: Learning without Overwriting: A Theory of Self-Distillation and Supervised Fine-Tuning in Continual Reasoning
authors: Shinichi Uemura, Taiji Suzuki
abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) of large language models (LLMs) has demonstrated the ability to improve reasoning capabilities while preserving previously acquired knowledge. Despite substantial empirical success, the dynamics of OPSD in continual reasoning remain incompletely understood. Modeling LLM reasoning as search over a directed acyclic graph, we provide a unified theoretical analysis of both the dynamics of post-training---OPSD and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) in continual learning---and the impact of pre-training on subsequent performance. Our findings establish three key insights with an optimization guarantee: (i) OPSD with hints from correct outputs enables continual learning without forgetting by sparse yet effective gradient descent updates induced by the hint structure. (ii) SFT on correct reasoning paths can lead to catastrophic forgetting due to dense updates along the training paths, which overwrite the information previously acquired. (iii) Diversity in pre-training is crucial for enabling a post-trained model to reach a correct output when a rollout starts from an intermediate state. Our results, supported by theoretical analysis, show that reliable continual reasoning depends on how post-training updates interact with the reasoning structure established during pre-training.

title: Poisson-GENERIC Neural Operators: Exact Metriplectic Structure in Function Space via Casimir Entropies
authors: Jason Sulskis, Sathya Ravi
abstract: Existing thermodynamically consistent neural operators enforce GENERIC degeneracy by projecting the reversible operator, introducing state dependence and generally forfeiting the Jacobi identity. We instead use the compatible Lie--Poisson pencil $L=\alpha D+\lambda(uD+Du)$ for nonlinear transport and constant Poisson multipliers otherwise. Augmenting $u$ with a latent entropy density $s$ makes $S=\int s$ a Casimir, so $L\,\delta S/\delta z=0$ without projection. The energy combines a fixed mechanical quadratic, a learned gauge-free potential, and a convex internal energy; the friction operator $M=AA^{\!\top}$ enforces $M\,\delta E/\delta z=0$ pointwise and supports diffusion and damping through local Onsager fluxes. Skewness, positivity, and both degeneracies hold algebraically for any parameters; the continuum pencil satisfies Jacobi, with discrete residuals at machine precision on alias-free inputs. Closed-form heat and damped-wave friction operators are exactly representable, and a discrete-gradient integrator preserves the first and second laws. Across four PDEs in one and two dimensions and three backbones (FNO, Transolver, CNO), the model wins $62/72$ seed-level comparisons against unconstrained baselines at equal optimizer steps, recovers exact transport and wave symbols, matches heat and Burgers dissipation within $12\%$, and dissipates nothing on advection. At equal wall-clock time, the unconstrained FNO is more accurate over ten frames. Over one hundred frames, in and out of distribution, our model never increases physical energy and conserves it when dissipation vanishes, whereas the unconstrained FNO loses a quarter of conserved energy out of distribution and projected GENERIC-FNO often creates energy. Limitations include late-time heat under-damping and explicit-integrator divergence on waves.

title: Not What a Child Expressed: Auditing the Sign-to-Text Safety Interface in Child-Facing AI
authors: Muhammad Rafiullah Memon, Viet Vo, Wanlun Ma, Yang Xiang
abstract: Automatic sign language translation (SLT) has entered consumer products, turning American Sign Language into English text for dictation, messaging, and queries put to a conversational assistant. Child-facing AI and platform trust-and-safety tooling decide on text, using filters on minor accounts and grooming classifiers that score chat messages. A signing child who uses SLT therefore reaches these safeguards through a translation. We found no publicly documented system in which the two have been jointly evaluated, and the leading deployed SLT model was neither trained nor formally evaluated on signers under 18. Errors that alter negation, participant roles, secrecy, urgency or help-seeking could change a safety decision without disturbing fluency. This paper proposes a Deaf-informed pre-deployment audit of that boundary, with a failure taxonomy, a sanitised scenario schema, four comparison conditions, and four outcome measures. Auslan is the planned first case study.

title: Can phenotypic activity be predicted without experimental readouts?
authors: T\'elio Cropsal, Roc\'io Mercado
abstract: Molecular encoders contrastively pretrained on paired molecule-morphology data, such as CLOOME and CellCLIP, have been proposed as cheap surrogates for phenotypic prediction, avoiding the need to run a Cell Painting assay. We evaluate this idea under a protocol designed to control for two confounds that can inflate apparent performance: leakage across an encoder's own pretraining boundary, and the correlation between phenotypic activity and simple cytotoxicity. Testing six representations, including a non-pretrained MLP control matching CLOOME's input and layer count, on two Cell Painting screens of different scale and origin, we find that once these confounds are controlled for, CLOOME and CellCLIP show no clear advantage over plain physicochemical descriptors, also under stricter activity definitions and with non-linear probes, and that toxicity is generally easier to predict than genuine phenotypic activity across representations. The protocol is not tied to these two models, and we suggest that leakage-aware, confound-controlled evaluation should be standard practice before phenotype-pretrained encoders are trusted as surrogates for predictive phenotypic drug discovery.

title: MINDSET: Energy-based Memory Evolution for Long Conversational Agents
authors: Sujato Dutta, Sreekruthy Tummala, Shashank Vanga, Ayushmi Pavani, BHVSP Subrahmanyam, Neeraj Choudhary
abstract: Long-term conversational memory requires more than retrieving past dialogue. A system must determine whether new evidence replaces an existing fact, applies in a different context or represents an unresolved contradiction. We introduce MINDSET, a local memory controller that makes these decisions without any LLM calls. It preserves original dialogue episodes and organizes them into provenance-linked, versioned schemas. For each incoming episode, a feasibility-constrained energy objective governs four possible transitions: reinforcement, supersession, contextual branching and new-schema creation. Stability rules prevent isolated conflicts from prematurely displacing established states while version links preserve access to historical evidence. At inference time, retrieval follows these structures back to original dialogue. On a frozen 700-question LoCoMo subset, MINDSET achieves the highest observed answer F1 among six evaluated systems and significantly improves retrieval ranking. Without retuning, it achieves the highest judge accuracy on LongMemEval knowledge-update cases, compared with the other baselines evaluated. Additional experiments with GLM-4.7 and Gemma-4-31B demonstrate compatibility across answer backbones. These results support explicit, non-generative memory-state control as an effective approach to address evolving conversational knowledge.

title: Finding Side-Effect Loopholes in AppWorld and WorkArena Verifiers
authors: Richard Abrich
abstract: Language-model agents act for people inside software, sending payments or editing records. Benchmarks such as AppWorld and WorkArena grade them with automated verifiers, whose verdicts also become reinforcement learning (RL) rewards, so a lenient verifier rewards mistakes. Verifier audits mostly hunt for runs that pass without doing the task; we ask about runs that do it and also change something nobody asked for. We mutation-test both verifiers with hand-written edits to correct runs, designed from the verifier source; an end-state check confirms each false positive. All confirmed false positives were unrequested changes; planted omissions and wrong values produced none. AppWorld's tests passed a duplicate write in all six tasks of two templates, and three RL methods that train on one of these templates would fully reward it; one count assertion per template rejected all six duplicates while passing every correct run. WorkArena's form verifier, called once after submission, passed all 36 edited runs that filled an unrequested field. Checked after every field, it caught extra fields filled first or in drop-downs but still passed all 8 runs that filled a text or reference field last. Both verifiers check that the requested change happened but not reliably that nothing else changed.

title: Beyond LLM-GA: Secure Fluid Antenna Systems with ReEvo-Designed Memetic Algorithm
authors: Hanyong Xu, Zhaolai Dang, Tong Zhang
abstract: Fluid antenna systems (FASs) offer significant spatial flexibility, yet securing them against eavesdropping is critical for practical FAS deployment in military, satellite, and internet-of-things networks. Although large language model (LLM)-assisted genetic algorithms (LLM-GAs) can address this secure FAS port selection problem, whether further algorithmic improvement is possible warrants deeper investigation. To this end, we propose a memetic algorithm based on reflective evolution (ReEvo). Unlike the state-of-the-art LLM-GAs, which design only crossover or mutation operators with an LLM, our algorithm leverages an LLM to evolve dedicated crossover, mutation, and local-search operators offline. These operators are then embedded into a memetic search framework, thereby obviating any online LLM queries during execution. Simulation results at equal generation counts demonstrate that our proposed algorithm achieves a higher secure sum-rate than the conventional GA and the state-of-the-art LLM-GAs.

title: QuSema: Detecting Silent Bugs in Quantum Libraries via Quantum-knowledge-enhanced Agents
authors: Yujin Song, Kaining Zhang, Qixin Zhang, Shuai Wang, Pingchuan Ma, Yuxuan Du
abstract: Quantum libraries are now critical infrastructure for quantum algorithm development, yet their correctness remains difficult to test. Existing testing techniques mainly rely on failure-based or comparison-based oracles, exposing bugs only when executions fail, violate runtime checks, or disagree with another implementation. Their applicability is limited when suitable execution-based oracles are unavailable, leaving some silent bugs undetected. Such missed bugs can produce incorrect results that propagate into experimental conclusions, simulation studies, and algorithmic designs. Here we present QuSema, an autonomous testing agent for finding silent bugs in quantum libraries. QuSema uses constraints from quantum semantics and documentation as a source-level semantic oracle to assess whether implementation logic can produce invalid outputs from valid inputs. It operates through an agentic loop that repeatedly inspects library API documentation and source code, reasons about the intended behavior of quantum operations, identifies potential semantic deviations, and validates them by generating executable tests through library APIs. Guided by quantum-domain reasoning, QuSema turns high-level behavioral mismatches into concrete, user-triggerable bug reports, enabling it to uncover non-crash defects. We implement QuSema for Qiskit and PennyLane. On a benchmark of 20 historical silent bugs, QuSema achieves higher mean bug relocation counts than Claude Code and Codex, with the DeepSeek configuration costing less than Claude Code. QuSema also discovers 40 previously unknown bugs confirmed by the developers, including 30 silent bugs.

title: Explaining the Saliency Map Sparsity of Adversarially-Trained Neural Networks
authors: Yannick Lunk, Atell Yehor Krasnopolsky, Damien Garreau, Leon Bungert
abstract: Understanding why deep neural networks make a given prediction is of great importance for their safe deployment. In computer vision, saliency maps, which highlight the image region most influential for a prediction, remain a widely-used form of explanation. An empirical observation is the apparent sparsity of gradient saliency maps of adversarially-trained neural networks. In this paper, we propose a theoretical explanation of this phenomenon for two-layer ReLU networks. We build on the established equivalence of adversarial training to the minimization of the empirical risk with weight-decay penalization and an added adversarial total variation term -- valid for certain loss functions. As the number of data points and neurons grows and the regularization parameters are sent to zero at appropriate rates, we prove that minimizers converge to a Bayes classifier with minimal gradient and Barron norm. Sparsity appears since for adversarial training with $\ell_\infty$-attacks the gradient norm is anisotropic and favors axis-aligned / sparse gradients. We illustrate our theoretical findings experimentally by evaluating the gradient $\ell_1$-norm and thresholded sparsity of naturally versus adversarially trained models.

title: VAMR: Multi-Question Agentic Reasoning for Efficient Long-Form Video Understanding
authors: Runquan Gui, Hanzhu Chen, Zehao Wang, Hanxin Zhu, Xin Li, Zhibo Chen
abstract: Long-form video understanding often involves multiple questions about different aspects of the same recording. Yet existing video agents typically process each question through an isolated tool-use trajectory. This repeatedly restarts video exploration and memory construction, missing opportunities to acquire evidence jointly and progressively build a shared understanding that supports the complete question set. We introduce \textbf{VAMR} (\textbf{V}ideo \textbf{A}gent for \textbf{M}ulti-Question \textbf{R}easoning), which coordinates all questions about a video through one shared tool-use trajectory. At each round, a persistent policy model can invoke tools for one or more unresolved questions and submit answers for questions with sufficient evidence. Question-conditioned visual perception retrieves fine-grained clues for several questions in one call, while layered multi-question memory integrates reusable context into a shared video story and preserves separate evidence for individual questions. After supervised fine-tuning initializes this interaction protocol, we propose question-horizon policy optimization (\qhpo) to optimize shared trajectories in which questions progress and finish at different rounds. Specifically, a question-level critic estimates the value of each active question, while round alignment maps each question advantage to the rounds that directly serve it before the aligned advantages are aggregated to optimize the shared actor. Across LVBench, Video-Holmes, and LongVideoBench, VAMR achieves the highest accuracy overall and the fewest reasoning rounds among iterative methods. On LVBench, it reaches 62.1\% accuracy, exceeding VideoARM by \textbf{4.3} points while reducing reasoning rounds and processed frames by \textbf{85.9\%} and \textbf{61.4\%}.

title: EvoKnow: Continual Knowledge Evolution for AI-Generated Image Detection
authors: Zhiheng Peng, Wenwei Jin, Yangshi Ge, Siyu Xia, Jiawei Li, Xu Tang
abstract: AI-generated image detectors are commonly trained on fixed generator domains and become difficult to maintain as new generative models emerge. Continual adaptation is challenging because replaying historical generated images is costly, whereas updating shared parameters with limited current-domain data can overwrite prior forensic knowledge. We propose EvoKnow, a replay-free framework that formulates continual AI-generated image detection as forensic knowledge evolution. EvoKnow preserves a shared forensic basis learned from base domains, incrementally adds isolated residual experts for complementary generator-relevant evidence, and retrieves expertise through an Analytical Incremental Router (AIR) updated in closed form from current-stage generated images and accumulated sufficient statistics. Experiments demonstrate effective cross-generator generalization, few-shot expansion, and long-horizon continual adaptation. With ten generated images per arriving generator, EvoKnow achieves 96.70% average accuracy on non-base GenImage generators and 94.48% accuracy on Chameleon without target-benchmark adaptation. Under a strict replay-free continual learning protocol, EvoKnow achieves state-of-the-art continual learning performance, attaining 96.32% mean stage-wise accuracy and 4.32% average forgetting.

title: Kernelized Parameter Sensitivity Atlases for Amortized Conditional Interpretability
authors: Davide Wiest, Ahanaf Hasan Ariq, Abdul Monaf Chowdhury
abstract: Gradient-based attribution provides input-specific information about model parameters, but computing it via backpropagation for many samples is expensive, while static importance scores discard input dependence. We derive KPSA (Kernelized Parameter Sensitivity Atlas) from a block decomposition of the empirical neural tangent kernel. It measures normalized parameter-group sensitivity, embeds those sources in an explicit query space, and uses a lightweight kernel to estimate sensitivities for unseen inputs. We derive bounds that separate finite-source from irreducible representation error and give margin-based top-$k$ recovery. This paper studies two interpretability applications. Firstly, KPSA identifies parameter groups with high susceptibility to perturbations across vision, forecasting, and protein-modeling setups. Across a fivefold range of parameter budgets ($0.02$-$0.1\%$), its selected groups attain $39$-$85\%$ of the perturbation susceptibility of a first-order backpropagation oracle. In vision and forecasting, these parameter groups form sparse sensitivity circuits that extend across depth and vary systematically with the input. Secondly, we use KPSA on an activation-attribution problem for MLP features in transformers. It retains $81\%$ of the gap between a backpropagation oracle and a constant-sensitivity baseline on vision while increasing batched query-time throughput from 551 to 2,041 images/s and reducing peak GPU memory from 4.55 to 0.44GB. On the protein-modeling task, it recovers $68\%$ of this gap. An ablation of KPSA's kernel aggregation shows that nearest-neighbor retrieval in KPSA space can remain competitive. The empirics show that compact kernel atlases can store useful input-dependent parameter sensitivity while amortizing repeated gradient attribution, a step toward scalable conditional interpretability. Code can be found at https://github.com/Axym-Labs/kpsa .

title: Unreliable Narrator Framing as a Cost-effective Mechanism for Satire Explanation of Australian and American Satirical News
authors: Kanay Gupta, David Y. Liu, Aditya Joshi
abstract: Satirical news is a unique form of misinformation: it is intended to be humorous by the original publication source but can be misinterpreted. Explanation of satirical news articles is challenging because recent and local context needs to be incorporated. This is a pilot study that explores explanation generation for satirical news articles from Australia and compares them alongside those from USA. We show that framing explanations with unreliable narrator theory on open-weight models can be a feasible, cost-effective alternative to frontier models. We find that models identify the satirical tropes more accurately on the American source than the Australian one. This work results in a novel dataset and an evaluation benchmark for satire explanation.

title: Lower Bounds for Randomized Linear-Oracle Optimization over Strongly Convex Sets
authors: Sebastian Pokutta
abstract: Recent results [arXiv:2602.04378, arXiv:2602.22608] establish lower bounds for optimization over strongly convex sets, covering specified Frank-Wolfe updates and unrestricted deterministic first-order linear minimization oracle (LMO) methods, respectively. Neither establishes a lower bound for unrestricted randomized methods. We close this gap by proving an $\Omega(L\operatorname{diam}(S)^2/T^2)$ distributional lower bound after $T$ oracle calls for randomized first-order LMO methods over strongly convex sets, with final outputs required to be feasible on every instance and seed. While our construction reuses the family of [arXiv:2602.22608], our proof characterizes the conditional distribution of the hidden permutation after adaptive queries and bounds the expected decrease of a combinatorial statistic controlling optimizer variance. We also show that the same error threshold holds with probability at least $3/4$ and yields a stopping-time tail bound. Our construction uses the same curvature-diameter coupling as [arXiv:2602.22608]. Comparisons with the upper bound [arXiv:1406.1305] must account for this coupling. Separately, we show that prescribed slow exact-line-search Frank-Wolfe trajectories can locally amplify sufficiently small initialization errors, corresponding to roughly one extra bit of initialization accuracy per iteration, and that initializations satisfying a particular eventual slow envelope have planar measure zero.

title: Where Polanyi Meets Galois: Tacit Knowing as an Algebro-Deterministic Operation, Toward Re-rooting AI-Generated Science
authors: Hiroyuki Chuma, Kanji Otsuka, Yoichi Sato, Kodo Yamauchi
abstract: Tacit knowing is an operating regime of memory, not a separate content. In VaCoAl (CASRAM, PyVaCoAl), a deterministic hyperdimensional memory over GF(2), one DAG of bound records is read in two ways. With all collisions repaired (Rescue), the trace is exactly auditable but no path outranks any; with collisions tolerated (Don't Care), a path confidence $CR_2$ ranks direct over circuitous routes unstated. This audit-valuation complementarity formalizes Polanyi's claim that tacit and explicit are not sharply divided. (1) Polanyi's from-to is non-commutative binding. (2) Full explication destroys the valuation (Lemma 1), as with Polanyi's pianist; tacitness is contingent or regime-bound, putting Polanyi, Nonaka, Tsoukas and Collins on one substrate. (3) The lemma answers the popular dual-process moral ("train slow System 2 to tame fast System 1"), mirroring the two-store reading of knowledge Polanyi rejected; Mercier and Sperber's reasoning as intuitive inference about reasons matches his. (4) To know a large DAG is to cull it. Against Polanyi's Meno reading, Simon held that a test and a generator, guided by statable heuristics, suffice. The AlphaGo-to-AlphaProof lineage builds the test, but its strongest systems cull by unstatable valuations: the tacit is relocated, not removed, results are verified yet rootless, and practicable traces must record the cull. (5) Collins's three tacit knowledges are bound structure, substrate valuation and value binding. (6) Our mentor-student DAG maps tacit transmission. (7) AI-solved problems lacking follow-ups (Tao) are rootless explicit knowledge, re-rooted if LLMs generate, VaCoAl traces, the community values. (8) For Mercier and Sperber an LLM is a sophist; truth-seeking lies in collective tacit knowing, Polanyi's conviviality, conjectured to extend beyond humans; machine-only knowledge reaches at most Sosa's animal grade. Testable predictions follow.

title: A Survey of Flow Matching in Reinforcement Learning
authors: Nabuat Zaman Nahim, Fairoz Nower Khan, Peizhong Ju
abstract: Flow Matching (FM) has recently emerged as a principled and efficient generative modeling framework for reinforcement learning (RL), enabling expressive, multimodal policy parameterizations via deterministic probability transport. Compared to diffusion-based policies that rely on stochastic denoising chains, FM uses sampling based on ordinary differential equations (ODEs), with learned velocity fields, which can substantially reduce inference latency and simplify the incorporation of RL objectives. As research in flow-based RL rapidly accelerates across offline continuous control, online fine-tuning, and foundation model alignment, the literature has become highly fragmented. In this survey, we provide a comprehensive taxonomy of flow-matching approaches in reinforcement learning. We organize the literature along two axes: the target distribution being modeled (e.g., action policies, value critics, transition dynamics) and the mechanism of RL signal integration (e.g., energy-weighted regression, flow-based policy gradients, and group relative policy optimization). Furthermore, we survey emerging frontiers such as discrete and non-Euclidean action spaces, provide a systematic comparative analysis against Gaussian and diffusion baselines, and outline critical open problems. Ultimately, this survey serves as a foundational roadmap for the next generation of generative reinforcement learning and alignment.

title: RFWeave: Generalizable Wireless Propagation Prediction Across Scenes and Transceiver Configurations
authors: Shurui Xu, Xiao Ye, Yijie Bian, Junjie Ai, Yuxuan Chen, Weicong Chen, Wei Guo, Wankai Tang, Jun Zhang, Shi Jin
abstract: Wireless propagation modeling is foundational to the evaluation and design of modern communication systems. While recent learning-based methods have shown promising generalization across transceiver positions and unseen scenes, they remain largely confined to a fixed configuration of array size, receiver orientation, and transmit beam. In this work, we introduce RFWeave, a unified feedforward model for wireless propagation prediction across scenes, transceiver positions, and transceiver configurations. Its core innovation is a flexible antenna representation that accommodates varying array structures while capturing spatial relations between transmitter and receiver elements. Our conditioning mechanism allows the model to use a shared Transformer backbone across diverse transceiver configurations, enabling joint prediction of received power and the angle-of-arrival spatial spectrum. Trained on a large-scale simulated dataset spanning 10,000 indoor scenes and more than 5 million channel records, RFWeave achieves state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of generalization settings, improving spatial spectrum structural similarity by up to 15.6% and reducing received power mean absolute error by up to 35.4% over the strongest baselines on unseen scenes. Additional experiments on measured DICHASUS data and in beam management further demonstrate RFWeave's broader applicability to real-world channels and downstream wireless tasks.

title: Making Tensor Decoupling More Robust and Less Parametric
authors: Maxime Rochkoulets, Joppe De Jonghe, Mariya Ishteva
abstract: Tensor decoupling algorithms recover compact representations of multivariate functions by combining linear factor matrices with univariate internal nonlinearities. We identify two limitations of recent methods. First, their performance is not invariant to mismatched output or gradient magnitudes, and second, their spline internals require manual tuning of their degrees of freedom. We propose two lightweight fixes. The first is a preprocessing step that rescales the input Jacobian tensor, removing both the bias towards larger magnitude outputs and the ill-conditioning of certain factor updates caused by such a mismatch. The second replaces B-spline internals by penalized splines coupled with generalized cross-validation, making the method less dependent on the user selecting the right number of control points. Finally, we release an efficient open-source JAX implementation of our algorithm.

title: Measuring Variable Importance Using Proportional Inclusive Marginal Effects
authors: Youngseo Cho, V. Roshan Joseph
abstract: Shapley-based measures are widely used for measuring variable importance in statistics and machine learning. However, these measures have a serious issue--a nonactive variable can get a positive importance measure when it is correlated with an active variable. Herin et al. recently proposed a measure called proportional marginal effects (PME) that mitigates this spurious effect. However, PME is developed for deterministic models and has high computational cost. In this article, we propose a new measure called proportional inclusive marginal effects (PRIME) that overcomes these two limitations of PME. The key idea in PRIME is to use a novel model-free variable selection technique to identify the active variables and include only them in the computation of the importance measure. Analysis of test functions and real datasets show that PRIME can accurately and reliably quantify variable importance from noisy input-output data.

title: Good human thinking populates AI's semantic blind spots
authors: Kibum Moon, Dan R. Johnson, Kostadin Kushlev, Oded Kleinmintz, Benjamin Lira, Indre Viskontas, James C. Kaufman, Roger E. Beaty, Nirav Patel, Emily Wenger, Angela L. Duckworth, Adam E. Green
abstract: AI-generated outputs tend to be more similar (homogenized) than human ideas. Does the human heterogeneity that extends beyond AI homogenization reflect valuable thinking that AI misses, or bad human ideas that AI avoids? We quantified how much an individual response expands an idea space beyond recurring clusters of ideas, enabling us to identify human responses located in AI's "semantic blind spots" (regions AI sparsely covers). Across three large samples (college admissions essays, alternative uses of objects, and interpersonal problem solving), human ideas in AI blind spots predicted higher academic achievement and performed as well or better on creativity, quality, and effectiveness. In contrast to humans, when AI expanded idea space, the association with creativity weakened or reversed. AI blind spots persisted across 66 diverse models and were not resolved by human-AI collaboration. Thinking "outside the bots" does not appear to reflect low-performing human variation that AI can safely omit.

title: SkillScreen: High-Recall Screening of Malicious Agent Skills with Decision Models
authors: Jerrold Huang, Junwei Quan, Saiyue Lyu, Zihan Guo, Yingqiang Ge
abstract: Agent skills turn natural-language instructions into actions, creating a security challenge: legitimate automation and malicious behaviour can look deceptively similar. A practical screen must catch nearly every attack while keeping the review load manageable. We present SkillScreen, a compact decision model trained to score skill maliciousness directly from SKILL$.$md in a single forward pass. On MaliciousSkillBench, SkillScreen flags 20-25% of benign skills at 99% recall on unseen attack families, substantially fewer than the word-level classifier and prompted LLM judges tested. Under the same training protocol, it also generalizes better than a fully fine-tuned encoder to unseen sources. Yet unfamiliar benign sources sharply increase false positives, showing that recognizing new attacks does not ensure reliable screening of new skill collections. Our results demonstrate the value of task-trained decision models for high-recall skill screening. Project page: https://jerroldh.github.io/SkillScreen-webpage/

title: Autonomous Science Bench: Evaluating AI Agents for Autonomous Scientific Discovery
authors: Yibo Wen, Han Liu
abstract: AI agents for autonomous scientific discovery must decide which experiments to run under a limited budget. Most benchmarks for science agents provide fixed datasets, while others that support active experimentation largely rely on simulation. We introduce Autonomous Science Bench, an initial release comprising six budgeted design-build-test-learn campaigns grounded in published experiments across biology, chemistry, and materials science. Agents select batches of designs, receive measurements from a lab service, and use the results to guide subsequent experiments before delivering a predictive model. Success requires passing two calibrated gates: a discovery gate, which evaluates the designs the agent measured, and a learning gate, which evaluates its model's ranking of held-out designs. In a pilot evaluation of ten agent-model configurations and 180 trials, the best configuration succeeds in 72% of trials, while the hardest campaign is solved in only five of 30 attempts. The two gates reveal different weaknesses: some agents build accurate rankings but find too few promising designs, while others find promising designs but fail to predict which unseen designs will perform well. These differences are obscured by overall success rates alone. We release version 0.1 of the campaigns, lab runtime, and public leaderboard at https://asb.open-ssi.org/.

title: Forecasting Brand Mentions in LLM Answers: Frozen Predictions Evaluated from Hours to Weeks
authors: Dmitrij \.Zatuchin
abstract: Companies and agencies now monitor which brands large language models (LLMs) name when buyers ask for recommendations. Answers vary between runs, so a single check can mislead and repeated checks cost money. We extend an earlier 20-day replication to ask how well past brand mentions predict later ones over seven weeks. We froze probabilistic forecasts before each of four prospective collection waves of Gemini 3.1 Pro answers to the same 54 buyer questions: nine question families in English, Estonian and Finnish, each for two markets, with four of 12 tracked brands per question. The waves were collected between 1.5 hours and 52 days after the history used by the earliest forecast, and each scored 648 brand and answer labels from 162 answers. A smoothed per-question history achieved a Brier score of 0.0599 at 1.5 hours, against 0.1131 for a per-brand rate and 0.25 for a constant 0.5. A pooled rate clipped to 0.05--0.95, named as the challenger before its first test, scored 0.0259 after 8 hours, 0.0269 after 30 days and 0.0328 after 52 days. Of the brand and question cells named in all or none of the earlier answers, 94.5% to 97.5% kept that pattern in each later wave, and none switched from always to never or back. With a search instruction, 100 of 162 answers returned search activity, compared with 1 of 540 earlier Pro answers; mentions stayed predictable (Brier 0.0563), and Pro history predicted a smaller model's answers less well (0.0787). Human coding agreed with 298/300 sampled automatic labels; two coders agreed on 99/100 shared items (kappa = 0.98). The results cover one provider family, a fixed candidate set and lexical mentions. They support per-question history as the baseline that any forecasting or monitoring method for LLM brand mentions should beat.

title: Learnable Hodge-Laplacian Driven Mixture of Experts for Steady-PDE Surrogates on Coarse Unstructured Meshes
authors: Stavros Nousias, Akis Nousias, Konstantinos Gkrispanis
abstract: Surrogate models approximate the solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs) for given geometries and boundary conditions. Conventional Transformer-based approaches typically employ a common feature-mixing mechanism across the solution domain, despite the presence of spatial variations at different scales. In this paper, we propose a mixture of transformer experts that combines a routing mechanism with multiscale supervision. Specifically, the individual experts are routed through a controller that utilizes learnable Laplacian matrices to compute weights, used to define a weighted sum of the experts for the output feature vectors at each point of the domain. Subsequently, a decoder receives the weighted sum of the experts output and predicts the solution fields. During training, the reference fields are decomposed into components at different spatial scales by repeated smoothing with a mesh Laplacian. We evaluate our approach on the official AirFRANS dataset using remeshed solution domains leading to unstructured triangular meshes of $4.9$k vertices. The experimental outcomes reveal lower mean relative $L_2$ error and interior mean squared errors among the compared models of this study. Code and data are publicly available in https://github.com/snousias/hodge-moe-pde

title: Latent Annealed Posterior Sampling with a Variance-Preserving Local Gaussian Approximation for Sparsely Observed Random Fields
authors: Jiankun Lei, Tian Qi, Xinping Yang, Xiaoting Gan
abstract: Posterior inference for random fields from sparse observations presents two major challenges: accurately characterizing complex spatial uncertainty and controlling conditional sampling costs as spatial resolution increases. We propose latent annealed posterior sampling (LAPS). LAPS first maps the random field into a lower dimensional latent space, while a Branch--Trunk coordinate decoder enables field evaluation at arbitrary spatial locations. Flow matching then learns the latent prior distribution. Based on this learned prior, LAPS performs posterior sampling through multilevel annealing. At each level, prior flow transport generates a reference state, which is combined with Gaussian noise using variance-preserving coefficients to construct a local Gaussian approximation of the conditional prior. This approximation is then combined with the observation likelihood to define a local posterior, from which latent posterior samples are generated using preconditioned MALA. Numerical experiments show that LAPS accurately approximates posterior distributions, preserves distinct posterior modes, and decouples posterior conditioning from output resolution. Across two Gaussian benchmarks, LAPS closely matches exact posterior references, with sliced Wasserstein distances $1.8\%$ and $2.4\%$ higher than those obtained from independent exact posterior samples. In the bimodal posterior benchmark, LAPS reduces the sliced Wasserstein distance from $0.2693$ to $0.1499$ and consistently recovers both modes across all test scenarios. For the two dimensional Navier--Stokes random field, LAPS substantially improves marginal posterior calibration while maintaining nearly constant evaluation time as the output grid is refined from $64^2$ to $192^2$. These results demonstrate that LAPS offers a favorable tradeoff among posterior accuracy, uncertainty calibration, and computational efficiency.

title: Wolof-Adapted Industry-Ready Open-Weight Language Models
authors: Gw\'enol\'e Lecorv\'e, Delphine Charlet, Pierre Adam, Floriane Behanzin, Lionel Delphin-Poulat, Johannes Heinecke, G\'eraldine Damnati, Pelin Kaytmaz, Noureddine Khaous, Charbel Kindji, Meriam Maadi, Abdoulaye Mbaye, Claire Perroux, Isma\"el Rousseau, Papa S\'ega Wad\'e, Gilles Xiberras, Olivier Zhang, Malek Zitouni
abstract: Wolof is spoken by 23M people, mostly in Senegal, but remains weakly supported by open-weight language models, while API models raise cost, governance, and sovereignty constraints for local deployments. In this paper, we present 0.6B-14B open-weight models adapted to Wolof through instruction tuning, preference alignment, and model merging. After presenting the pipeline and data, extensive experiments on 63~public and in-house tasks show good performance on Wolof understanding and generation while remaining effective on other languages and cross-lingual skills, with the 8B and 14B models being particularly competitive with substantially larger commercial systems. The models are currently being evaluated in internal customer-care pilots and are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/collections/Orange/wolof-lm .

title: Noise-Space Reward Alignment for Few-Step Generative Models
authors: Woocheol Shin, Taeyoung Yun, Jiwon Sung, Hyeongyu Kang, Jeongmin Park, Jaewoo Lee, Kyuil Sim, Dohyun Kim, Yutong He, Jinkyoo Park
abstract: Few-step generative models produce high-quality samples in one or a few evaluations. However, steering them toward desired properties remains difficult, especially when only black-box reward evaluations are available. While one could apply approaches developed for iterative diffusion and flow-based models, such as direct RL fine-tuning or test-time scaling, we find that neither transfers well to the few-step regime: direct fine-tuning suffers from severe reward over-optimization, and test-time scaling sacrifices the efficiency advantage of few-step generation. We propose Noise Policy Optimization (NPO), which explicitly targets the alignment problem for few-step generative models. The key idea is to learn an amortized flow policy over the initial noise space of the generator. The trained policy transports Gaussian noise to a reward-tilted noise distribution, whose pushforward distribution through the frozen generator is exactly the reward-tilted output distribution. By keeping the generator frozen, we can effectively utilize the knowledge encoded in the pretrained model, yielding a better reward-quality trade-off than direct fine-tuning. The amortized policy moves the search cost into training, so inference adds only a lightweight noise sampling step on top of the pretrained model. To improve sample efficiency during training, we use ELBO-based likelihood estimation that requires only sampled endpoints rather than simulated trajectories. Across image, language, and protein structure generation, NPO consistently achieves a better reward-quality trade-off than direct fine-tuning, and matches test-time search methods with 16 to 549 times lower inference cost.

title: Does On-Policy Distillation Need to Complete Every Rollout?
authors: Zhengxin Zhang, Maosen Tang, Ning Wang, Changhao Li, Jingren Zhou, Bo Dai, Sainyam Galhotra, Alex Townsend, Claire Cardie
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher knowledge to a student through feedback on student-generated rollouts, but generating complete rollouts and computing per-token teacher feedback are computationally expensive. Existing truncation methods save computation by stopping rollouts early. However, they do not compensate for truncated token gradients, which biases the gradient estimates and changes Vanilla OPD's original training objective. Furthermore, their truncation decisions rely on assumptions about supervision quality or criteria that may not generalize across settings. We introduce Stochastic Truncated On-Policy Distillation (STOPD), which accelerates OPD by randomly truncating student rollouts and correcting the resulting sampling bias with blockwise inverse-probability weighting (IPW). At each training step, we sample a stopping position for each rollout before generation and let the student generate until that position or natural termination. We obtain teacher feedback on every generated token and use blockwise IPW to compensate for the lower probability of retaining later tokens while controlling the weights. We prove that this weighting preserves Vanilla OPD's gradient sum in expectation and derive one-step update-error bounds for SGD, Adam, and Muon. We evaluate STOPD across multiple teacher-student model pairs, task domains, and optimizers. STOPD reduces generated tokens by 25-48% while maintaining accuracy comparable to Vanilla OPD, achieving 1.3-2.2x training speedups.

title: PriorityFEC: Deadline-Aware Streaming FEC for KV-Cache Handoff in Edge Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Han Shen, Qifu Tyler Sun, Fanyang Meng, Ye Wang, Yongsheng Liang
abstract: Collaborative edge large language model (LLM) systems often require repeated prefill computation when task contexts are transferred between agents. Reusing previously computed key--value (KV) caches can eliminate this overhead, but requires KV-cache delivery before the receiving agent begins decoding. Under strict deadlines and unreliable edge links, complete KV cache transfer may be infeasible, making the timely delivery of useful KV information critical. This paper proposes PriorityFEC, a utility-aware KV-cache handoff scheme that combines prioritized source transmission with adaptive loss recovery. PriorityFEC first organizes KV blocks into a utility-aware source queue to prioritize important information. It then employs ACK-sliding Streaming FEC and a lightweight Double Deep Q-Network (Double-DQN) scheduler to dynamically balance source delivery and repair transmission under deadline constraints. We implement PriorityFEC in a distributed edge LLM-serving prototype and evaluate it using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across multiple workloads. Experimental results demonstrate that PriorityFEC preserves more useful KV information and achieves substantially higher task accuracy than competing transport schemes, particularly when the deadline is insufficient to deliver the complete KV cache.

title: Cross-Precision Transfer, Non-Local Context, and Capacity-Readout Boundaries of Scale Calibration in Low-Bit LLMs
authors: Xu Cao, Wenxuan Xiao
abstract: Low-bit post-training quantization freezes integer codes and zero points, leaving groupwise scales as a compact adaptation interface. We study cross-precision transfer, non-local context, optimizer capacity, and readout behavior on Qwen3-1.7B and Llama-3.2-3B. First, transferring relative scale gains between floating-point and INT3 Qwen models with zero recipient training retains 76.9%-90.5% of self-calibration NLL reductions on fresh WikiText and C4, alongside resolved own-source preferences. Group permutation destroys transfer, and norm-matched layer withdrawal degrades all 16 layer-domain comparisons. A Llama control with identical initial tensors at all calibrated projections isolates preferences induced by surrounding network context. Second, expanding Llama calibration from 4 to 196 projections (0.79M to 22.02M scales) makes learning rate 0.01 win a 50-step training-loss pilot. Continuing to 200 steps memorizes the 28-block WikiText pool, inflates unseen perplexity by 2.06-2.28 times relative to 4-site calibration, and degrades mixed-action PIQA accuracy; learning rate 0.001 prevents memorization and restores accuracy. Third, across 24 Qwen ARC readout endpoints, advancing from 200 to 600 steps worsens INT3 teacher KL on plain-text readouts yet improves it under chat wrapping. Cross-fitted four-parameter static option bias explains 71.4%-75.4% of quantized Chat-Space score-shift SSE, versus less than 2.3% on floating point. Subtracting this bias raises INT3 chat teacher agreement from 33.3%-33.9% to 56.6%-57.5% and cuts KL from 4.15-4.42 to 1.18-1.24 nats.

title: Look Back, Correct Forward: Error Feedback Calibration for Time Series Forecasting
authors: Haonan Yang, Yulin He, Zhuo Li, Jing Zhao, Huibin Tan
abstract: Time series forecasting models are increasingly deployed in continuously evolving environments. After a forecast is issued, future observations gradually arrive and reveal how the model has failed. Existing methods mainly treat such observations as supervision for parameter updates. However, it remains unclear whether verified forecasting errors can themselves provide causal feedback for correcting future predictions. To address this, we introduce Error Feedback Calibration (EFC), a fully test-time framework for deterministic post-hoc correction of time series forecasting. EFC constructs a Causal Error Diagonal (CED) from revealed errors of overlapping historical forecasts, providing a fresh view of the frozen forecaster's recent failure behavior. Then Cumulative Error Transport (CET) maps this error state to future residuals using cumulative estimation, while temporal out-of-sample validation controls the correction strength. Temporal Residual Learning (TRL) further predicts only the residual structure left after CET from recent CED trajectories, rather than relearning the entire forecasting error. Extensive experiments across forecasting backbones and datasets show that EFC broadly improves forecasting performance while substantially controlling harmful over correction.

title: When the Editing Intent Is Split: A Cross-Modal Jailbreak Attack for Large Image Editing Models
authors: Xianmin Ye, Zhiyuan Fan, Tianju Liu, Yuhang Wang, Zhenxing Niu, Haichang Gao
abstract: Large image editing models increasingly infer editing intent from both textual and visual inputs, creating an underexplored safety risk when harmful intent is distributed across modalities. In this work, we formalize this split-intent vulnerability and propose the Split-Intent Jailbreak Attack (SIJA), which asymmetrically distributes an unsafe editing intent by specifying the editing referent in text while concealing the safety-critical action and specification through graphical visual semantics in an auxiliary cue. To systematically study this threat, we introduce the Split-Intent Image Editing Safety Benchmark (SI2ESBench) for evaluating image editing models under split-intent inputs. Extensive experiments on representative commercial and open-source models demonstrate that SIJA effectively compromises state-of-the-art image editing systems, achieving ASRs of 68.28% on GPT Image 2 and 91.38% on Qwen-Image-3.0-Pro. Our results expose a mismatch between multimodal editing and safety assessment: the distributed intent can be recovered to execute the requested transformation, yet its harmfulness often remains undetected by existing safeguards. To mitigate this vulnerability, we propose editing-intent reconstruction, a defense principle that explicitly evaluates the complete transformation implied by the joint multimodal context and substantially improves rejection of split-intent attacks. Our findings expose a cross-modal safety gap in modern image editing systems and highlight the need to assess the jointly inferred transformation rather than individual inputs in isolation. Project page: https://github.com/yexianmin/SIJA.

title: Announced Breaks Separate Conformal Reliability from Frequency Calibration
authors: Karl Li
abstract: When the process behind a time series changes on an announced date, like Australia's switch to five minute electricity settlement on October 1, 2021, intervals calibrated before it can stop covering at their stated level. Whether a forecaster needs the next interval to cover or a finished period's share of misses on target decides the restart. We recompute the next conformal interval from post-break forecast errors, and for n independent ones from the same continuous law, its expected coverage error is $O(n^{-1/2})$, the optimal order in a fixed class among methods told the date. For a finished period's share of misses to match its target, we restart adaptive conformal inference (ACI), which on bounded errors brings that share within $O(n^{-1})$ of target if its corrections at a lower limit stay bounded in total, for that period only. After a simulated mean jump of 5.0 standard deviations, recomputed 90% intervals lie an expected 3.5 percentage points from target at the 50th forecast, a third closer than the 5.2 of the best of five adaptive methods. Of 9 announced changes in Texas, Australian and PJM power markets and a Federal Reserve decision, only Australia's switch moves the errors enough for a 5% test at 80% power to resolve a gain from restarting ACI, and dates help restarted ACI only after large changes.

title: Inside the Loop: A Mechanistic Study of Looped Transformers on Permutation Traversal
authors: Magnus Sesodia, Juil Sock, Philip Torr, Christian Schroeder de Witt
abstract: Solving algorithmic tasks with many sequential steps typically requires scaling up transformer depth or chain-of-thought length, incurring unfavorable parameter and inference-compute costs, respectively. Looped transformers, which reuse one block of layers across many iterations, are poised to address this, since they scale effective depth without adding parameters or tokens. Yet, it remains unclear what each iteration is actually computing, or whether the loop merely simulates a deeper untied stack. Here, we study directed permutation traversal, in which a model follows H hops from a starting node and reports the node it reaches, so every intermediate hop has a known ground truth. We find that a minimum effective depth is necessary to solve the task, beyond which the degree of weight tying becomes the determining factor. For instance, a looped transformer with a four-layer block iterated eight times solves the task in every seed, while an identically trained untied transformer of the same effective depth never does, succeeding only with a lower learning rate or supervision of its intermediate layers. Probing and intervening on the residual stream, we find that the looped model advances through the intermediate nodes gradually, forming a staircase that adapts to its iteration budget, whereas the untied model, at that lower rate, exposes them only in its final layers. Taken together, our results recast looped transformers as iterative program learners, which allocate their iterations to successive steps of the algorithm and solve tasks that identically trained untied models of the same effective depth do not. Code is available at https://github.com/magnus-sesodia/insidetheloop.

title: Who Plans, Who Edits? Verified, Cost-Aware Division of Labor for LLM-Driven Analog Layout Repair
authors: Xilai Dai, Saeed Mohammadi
abstract: Language-model agents can repair analog layouts when sign-off tools check every edit, but which model should plan a repair, which should edit it, and at what cost remain open questions. In our tool-grounded repair agent, models only choose bounded layout operators; sign-off tools rerun each task's contract checks after every edit, so failing layouts are never accepted. On layout-versus-schematic (LVS), design-rule checking (DRC), and post-layout repairs of three designs (a production high-voltage digital-to-analog converter (DAC), a 5-V oscillator, and a SKY130 operational transconductance amplifier (OTA)) with six tier-matched models from two vendors, 182 blind runs show that cheap models execute plans but rarely succeed alone (the cheapest model: 1 of 11 runs alone, 16 of 17 under a flagship planner; p < 0.001), cheap planners fail more often, and no fixed assignment is cheapest on every task. We propose a learning controller that selects models for each role and the escalation order from the first tool evaluation and updates Bayesian estimates after every attempt. With rules and initial estimates frozen before testing, the controller fixed 7 of 8 episodes on four sealed held-out tasks, matching the OpenAI flagship alone, at 15-40% of the flagship's spend per fix on three tasks but 8% higher spend overall. The cheapest mid-tier model alone fixed 6 of 8 at the lowest overall spend per fix but missed the hardest task. All 32 extracted DAC repairs match the human-guided LVS repair's integral nonlinearity (INL) within 0.005 least significant bits (LSB) at every code.

title: World Models, Trees and Foundation Models for Retail Forecasting: Evidence from Four Public Data Sets
authors: Karthik Iyer, Madan Dabbeeru
abstract: A retailer makes different decisions at different grains of the product, store and time hierarchy: store orders for an item in a store, supplier funding for an item across stores, category performance by store, and the financial plan for the chain. Which forecasting model to use depends on the grain. This paper compares models at each grain on four public data sets (M5, six Dominick's categories, Breakfast at the Frat, and Corporaci\'on Favorita, the last kept out of all development), over rolling forecast origins with paired tests and model confidence sets. It covers price and promotion through the plan inputs these data record, not product, assortment or place. The models are a world model that carries each item's state forward under the price and promotion plan, the same network without that state, LightGBM, the Temporal Fusion Transformer, TimesFM, Chronos-Bolt, Timestral, seasonal naive, and an equal-weight average of the world model, LightGBM and TimesFM given the plan. The answer changed with the grain. For an item by store and an item across stores, the average had the lowest error on seven and eight of nine data sets, and the 90% confidence set held a median of 1 and 2 models. For a category by store, a category and the chain total, the lowest-error model differed between data sets and a median of 4 of nine models were not separated by the four to six windows available. For category-by-store planning cost, the average or LightGBM was lowest on seven of eight data sets, and the world model was lowest only on M5; it was behind LightGBM item by store on six of eight.
